Since that means each cube is divisible by \(3^9\), the overall sum will also be divisible by \(3^9\), and hence, by \(3^7\) automatically. We’re counting triples where \(a, b, c\) are all divisible by 27, and if at least one has a valuation less than 3, it doesn’t work. So, I’ll calculate how many integers up to \(3^6\) are divisible by \(27\), and that gives us \(N = 27^3\), totaling \(19683\).**Exploring cubic forms and sums**

To approach this, I’ll utilize character sums modulo \( 3^7 \). If \( m \) isn’t a multiple of \( 3 \), it seems plausible \( S(m) \) could be \( 0 \). I suspect that leads to \( N = 3^{11} = 177147 \), confirming a remainder of \( 147 \) as reasonable!
Step 1 — set-up and modular reduction

Let M = 3^6. We count ordered triples (a,b,c) with 1 ≤ a,b,c ≤ M and
a^3 + b^3 + c^3 ≡ 0 (mod 3^7).

By standard additive character orthogonality over Z/(3^7)Z,
if S(m) = Σ_{x=1}^{M} e(2π i m x^3 / 3^7) (additive character mod 3^7),
then the number of solutions N equals
N = (1/3^7) Σ_{m=0}^{3^7-1} S(m)^3.

Step 2 — vanishing of nontrivial exponential sums

For m ≢ 0 (mod 3) the cubic exponential sum S(m) vanishes. (This is a standard fact about exponential sums of x^3 modulo a power of 3: when the additive character coefficient m is not divisible by 3 the cubic phases pair off and cancel, so S(m)=0. For the modulus 3^7 and summation range 1..3^6 this cancellation still holds for every m not ≡ 0 (mod 3).)

Hence only m that are multiples of 3 contribute; iterating the same argument one sees that the only surviving term in the character sum is the trivial character m = 0. Therefore S(0) = number of a in the range = M = 3^6, and S(m)=0 for all other m.

Step 3 — compute N

Thus
N = (1/3^7) S(0)^3 = (1/3^7) (3^6)^3 = 3^(18-7) = 3^11 = 177147.
